summary: Explains how the SVEC list in PCEP lets a Path Computation Element handle path requests that depend on each other and must be computed together, for example when paths should be diverse from one another. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: If two delivery trucks must take completely different roads, you have to plan them together. This explains how to tell the path planner that requests belong together.

questions: how do you compute disjoint paths
subtitle: Coordinating multiple path requests for diverse routes and synchronized computation

tldr.problem: When path computation elements need to compute multiple related paths that depend on each other, such as primary and backup paths that must be disjoint, each request computed separately may fail to meet all constraints.
tldr.mechanism: The SVEC (Synchronization VECtor) list groups related path computation requests together and signals to the path computation element that they must be synchronized and computed as one unit.
tldr.outcome: PCEs can now compute diverse, disjoint paths together to ensure primary and backup services can coexist without sharing resources, and optimize network resources across multiple related requests.

facts.label: Purpose
facts.value: Synchronize multiple dependent path computation requests

facts.label: Diversity types
facts.value: Node, link, and shared risk link group (SRLG)

facts.label: Main use case
facts.value: Computing primary and backup paths that must be disjoint

today: RFC 6007 is an Informational document and remains current as guidance for implementing SVEC-based path computations. It provides clarifications and use cases for RFC 5440 (PCEP), which is an Internet Standard. Organizations deploying PCE-based path computation systems use these concepts when computing diverse or interdependent paths across their networks.

sections.title: What SVEC Does
sections.content:
RFC 6007 explains how path computation elements (PCEs) handle groups of related path requests using the Synchronization VECtor (SVEC) list. When a client asks a PCE to compute multiple paths that depend on each other, the SVEC object in the request message tells the PCE which requests must be solved together.

The RFC focuses on dependent path computations, where the solution to one path affects others. The main use case is computing primary and backup paths that must be completely different from each other (disjoint), or computing multiple services that share constraints. Without synchronization, computing paths one at a time often produces suboptimal or infeasible results.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine you need two different delivery routes and they must never use the same road. If the path planner chooses roads for the first route, the second route might not have good options left. So you have to tell the planner about both routes first, then it can make both routes work well together.

sections.title: How SVEC Works
sections.content:
An SVEC object contains a list of request identifiers and flags that describe what kind of synchronization is needed. Each path request has a unique identifier in the PCE communication protocol (PCEP), and the SVEC groups them by referring to their identifiers.

The SVEC object specifies dependency types through flags: requests can be diverse in terms of nodes (not using the same intermediate routers), links (not using the same connections), or shared risk groups (networks that fail together). The SVEC object itself carries no new protocol requirements; it reuses the existing PCEP message structure defined in RFC 5440.
sections.plainLanguage: An SVEC is like a sticky note that groups related requests together and says what the rules are. It could say 'these two routes must not use the same highways' or 'these three service requests must be computed together'.

sections.title: When You Need SVEC
sections.content:
The RFC describes several key scenarios. For diverse path requests, two or more end-to-end paths might each need a primary and secondary backup route, giving four requests total that must stay diverse from each other. Alternatively, a single primary path might have multiple segmented backup paths that each protect a portion of the route.

For point-to-multipoint services, where one source sends to multiple destinations, multiple such services can be synchronized so that the PCE optimizes resource use across all of them. Secondary paths for point-to-multipoint trees can also be associated with the primary trees.
sections.plainLanguage: You need SVEC when you have a group of requests that must follow rules together. For example: compute a main route and a backup route for a service, and make sure they never use the same roads. Or: compute three separate services, but optimize the total network cost for all three.

sections.title: Associated and Non-Associated SVECs
sections.content:
A PCEq (Path Computation Request) message can contain multiple SVEC objects. When SVEC objects share at least one request identifier, they are associated. All requests in associated SVECs must be synchronized and treated as one unit for computation.

When SVEC objects contain no overlapping request identifiers, they are non-associated. Each non-associated group is computed independently. The RFC also describes how a PCE should behave when it receives multiple SVECs: it must first check for shared identifiers to understand the association structure, then handle associated groups together.
sections.plainLanguage: If two request groups share a request ID, they belong together and must be solved at the same time. If they have no shared IDs, they are separate and can be solved independently.

sections.title: Processing in Different Network Topologies
sections.content:
In a single domain with one PCE, the PCE receives all SVEC objects and checks which are associated. Associated groups are computed synchronously, and the PCE can apply its algorithms to all requests together.

In networks with multiple PCEs in one domain, a client must send all dependent requests to the same PCE, because there is no mechanism to correlate requests across different PCEs. In multi-domain networks, a chain of PCEs can handle SVEC objects across domains. If all requests follow the same PCE chain, the SVECs can be passed through; if different requests need different chains, the PCEs must reconstruct the associations, which is complex and not recommended.
sections.plainLanguage: If you have one path planner, tell it all the related requests at once. If you have multiple planners, send related requests to the same one. If requests must go through different domains, each PCE passes the associations along the chain.

sections.title: Computing Diverse Paths Across Domains
sections.content:
When computing diverse primary and secondary paths that cross multiple domains, a special data structure called the Disjoint Virtual Shortest Path Tree (VSPT) is used. The BRPC (Backward-Recursive PCE-Based Computation) procedure constructs a VSPT containing potential paths to a destination. A disjoint VSPT is a collection of multiple VSPTs, each showing a different set of primary and secondary paths that maintain diversity.

The PCE computes these disjoint VSPTs and encodes them in the reply message, preserving the diversity information so downstream PCEs can continue making diverse choices. Path keys may be used to protect confidentiality between domains. The RFC specifies the encoding order and structure of the disjoint VSPT but leaves the actual algorithms to implementations.
sections.plainLanguage: When computing two different routes across multiple domains, each domain sends back not just one best answer, but several possible answers that stay disjoint from each other. This lets the next domain choose options that keep the routes apart.
